did.unittitle: Esmond Bradley Martin collection of correspondence related to Zanzibar
did.abstract: Collection of 15 handwritten and typed letters, dating from 1838 to 1937, written by the rulers of the Sultanate of Zanzibar, the King of Johanna (Anjouan), various British colonial officials and Zanzibari officials, which were collected by the American wildlife conservationist Esmond Bradley Martin.

accessrestrict.head: Conditions governing access
accessrestrict.p: The Esmond Bradley Martin collection is open and available for use in the Archives and Special Collections department of the New York University Abu Dhabi Library.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The correspondence in the Esmond Bradley Martin collection is arranged in one series, chronologically by the dates on each letter.

bioghist.head: Biographical note
bioghist.p: Esmond Bradley Martin (1941-2018) was an American geographer, researcher, and wildlife conservationist who became best known in the latter decades of his life for his work in researching and identifying networks of the illegal trade in rhinoceros horns and elephant ivory, a trade that had led to a precipitous decline in the populations of those animals in their African habitats. His efforts led to a sharp reduction in the ivory trade, and to efforts in China to outlaw the trade in rhinoceros horns (1993) and ivory (2017).

Born into a wealthy family in New York City on 17 April 1941 (his great-grandfather was steel magnate Henry Phipps, an associate of Andrew Carnegie), Martin attended the Brooks School (North Andover, Massachusetts), from which he graduated in 1959, and then earned bachelor's and master's degrees in agricultural economics from the University of Arizona in 1964. He pursued a doctoral degree from the University of Liverpool, with his dissertation, which he defended in 1970, focused on the historical development of the city of Malindi, on the Indian Ocean coast of Kenya. Martin and his wife Chryssee then moved to Kenya in the mid-1970s, where they conducted further historical and anthropological research, and where they built a house in the Nairobi suburb of Langata.

Martin's historical interest in the patterns of Indian Ocean trade, and in particular those of the merchants who traveled from Arabia to the east coast of Africa on dhows, the traditional sailing vessels of the region, eventually led him to an interest in researching the illicit trade in wildlife products, in particular, that of ivory from elephants and rhinoceros horns, the latter of which various cultures prized for their supposed aphrodisiac qualities, or for their use as decorative elements, such as on Yemeni daggers. In 1979 the World Wildlife Fund asked Martin to conduct research on the illegal ivory trade, and this led him to the career that he pursued for the next four decades, researching the paths of this illicit trade and campaigning to protect elephants and rhinoceroses by outlawing this trade.

Martin died at his home near Nairobi on 4 February 2018, after having been stabbed by an unidentified intruder. While the local police ruled it to have been a murder that resulted from a botched robbery, others suspected that Martin may have been targeted due to his work combating poachers and traders of ivory and rhinoceros horns.

During their time in Kenya, the Martins assembled an extensive library of rare books, prints, and archival documents related to the history of the "Swahili Coast" of Kenya and Tanzania, as well as Africa more generally. Many of these items were auctioned by Doyle Auctioneers in New York in November 2023.

custodhist.head: Custodial history
custodhist.p: These documents were collected from various sources by Esmond Bradley Martin, and were in his possession at the time of his death in 2018. Along with the other contents of his personal library, they were offered for sale by Doyle Auctioneers in New York in November 2023, and since then, many of the items from this auction have reached the antiquarian trade, including this grouping of letters, which were purchased by the NYU Abu Dhabi Library in May 2024.

scopecontent.head: Content Description
scopecontent.p: The Esmond Bradley Martin collection of correspondence related to Zanzibar consists of 15 handwritten and typed letters, dating from 1838 to 1937, written by the rulers of the Sultanate of Zanzibar, the King of Johanna (Anjouan), British and American diplomats, and Zanzibari officials, which were collected by the American wildlife conservationist and scholar Esmond Bradley Martin as part of his personal library, and kept at his home in Nairobi.

As items that were likely collected by Martin over the course of several years, if not decades, there is no single overarching theme in the collection, but rather, glimpses of the various aspects of the activities of rulers in the western Indian Ocean region--chiefly Zanzibar--as they encountered Western diplomats, merchants, and colonial officials in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Most of the correspondence consists of autograph letters signed (ALS), either in Arabic or English. Most frequently, the rulers hand wrote their letters in Arabic, often including a signet stamp, and either a later British official or collector added an English translation of the contents, attaching that to the original letter.

The earliest letter, an autograph letter signed from the Busaidi ruler Saʻīd bin Sulṭān in September 1838, just a few years after the Sultan had moved his seat of power from Muscat to Zanzibar, was addressed to the American consul Richard P. Waters, a merchant from Salem, Massachusetts, whose appointment represented a pivotal moment in Omani relations with the United States, reflecting the growing interest of Salem-based merchants in this part of the world. In Sultan Saʻīd's letter, he acknowledged the request from the captain of an American merchant ship who wished to meet with the him, which he was pleased to do.

Subsequent correspondence from British diplomats pointed to the growing slave trade that was based in Zanzibar, which the British government wished to stop. An 1843 letter from the British consul in Zanzibar, Atkins Hamerton, was given to the captain or crew of a ship traveling to Aden, in order to vouch for the legitimacy of this voyage, in case the vessel was stopped by Royal Navy ships searching for slave traders. An 1864 letter from a later British consul in Zanzibar, R. Lambert Playfair, which was copied and sent between British officials based in Bombay, contained observations about the seeming decline in the slave trade following a recent British decree banning the shipment of slaves during the monsoon season. Playfair noted that "slave vessels which formerly passed daily under the windows of my house are now never seen" and that "the slave market is almost empty."

A number of letters between the 1860s and 1870s show the role of Sultan Mohammed bin Ahmad al-Alawi, and other members of the local ruling class in Zanzibar--whose role as rulers had predated the arrival of the al-Busaidis--issuing rulings in local cases involving property disputes and other similar matters. Later correspondence from the 1880s shows some of the sons of Sultan Saʻīd, such as Barghash, Khalifah, and 'Ali, some of whom were to succeed him as Sultan, playing a similar role in arbitrating disputes. Since none of those latter pieces of correspondence have the ruler's signet stamp on them, one might assume that this correspondence predates their accession to the role of Sultan.

One outlier in this group of correspondence--and the only one that does not reference Zanzibar--is an 1867 letter from Abdullah, the King of Johanna, which is the present-day Anjouan in the Comoros Islands. He wrote to the British colonial ruler in Aden, asking that he assist his brother in his travels to Bombay, noting that "he is an entire novice in regard to travelling as this is the first time he has left the island."

The last letters in this collection consist of the Arabic original, along with an English handwritten translation, of a letter from one of the last Sultans of Zanzibar, Khalīfah ibn Ḥārib, written in 1937 to the British author Harold Ingrams, who had earlier served as the acting Colonial Secretary in Zanzibar, and who had recently congratulated Sultan Khalifah on his silver jubilee. The Sultan thanked Ingrams for this, and made reference to his planned visit to London to attend the coronation of King George VI later that same year.

userestrict.head: Conditions governing use
userestrict.p: The copyright status of the documents in this collection is unknown. Due to the age of these documents, it is likely that the copyright term for most of these materials has expired, yet it is ultimately the responsiblity of individual researchers to investigate the copyright status of such works for any intended uses that would exceed the common definitions of "fair use."
